variants.name: scala.concurrent Promise + Future callbacks
variants.implementation_notes: The standard library supplies both halves of the pattern: a Promise is a writable, single-assignment token that the completing side (service callback, actor, timer) fills in with success/failure, and the client's Future.onComplete/foreach callbacks are the demultiplexed completion actions, so no registry keyed on request identity is needed. In protocols without a reply address, keep a Map[requestId, Promise] - that map is exactly the client-side token table of the classic pattern. Where the service is an actor or an effect, the token travels with the request instead (see the Akka ask and cats-effect variants).
variants.code_sketch:
val token = Promise[Reply]()                 // the ACT the service will complete
outstanding.put(req.id, token)               // only for protocols without a replyTo
token.future.onComplete {
  case Success(r) => handle(req, r)
  case Failure(e) => fail(req, e)
}
transport.send(req)
pitfalls: A Promise is single-assignment: success/failure/complete on a completed promise throws IllegalStateException, so racing completers must use trySuccess/tryFailure/tryComplete and accept schedule-dependent outcomes.

Callbacks on one future are unordered and may run concurrently, and blocking inside them starves the ExecutionContext (ForkJoinPool) unless wrapped in blocking - completion handlers must stay non-blocking.
There is no leak of callbacks once they have run, but a promise that is never completed and never removed from the registry retains its state forever.

variants.name: Akka/Pekko typed ask with a replyTo address
variants.implementation_notes: In an actor system the token is the reply address: a typed ask creates a temporary ActorRef[Response] and embeds it in the request as replyTo, so the response is delivered straight to the requester's continuation - the pattern's object-reference representation, and the reason the protocol needs no correlation ids. Inside an actor, context.ask adapts the reply into a message; outside, AskPattern.ask returns a Future. Choose it where blocking on a Future inside an actor is unacceptable; the cost is a temporary actor and a mandatory timeout per request.
pitfalls: Every ask needs an implicit Timeout: without it, no response means an indefinitely pending token (the ask itself fails with TimeoutException when the timeout fires).
The reply-adaptation function may run after the actor's state changed - close over immutable values, not over mutable fields.
Asking from inside an actor in a request/response cycle creates the actor equivalent of a callback chain: unbounded outstanding asks turn into memory growth and deadlock risk.

variants.name: cats-effect IO.async callback registration
variants.implementation_notes: Effect systems express the same registration functionally: IO.async hands the producer a completion callback (Either[Throwable, A] => Unit) that must be run exactly once, and IO.cancelable adds the cancellation half, so the token is the callback plus a finalizer that tries to abandon the outstanding operation. ZIO's Promise plus fiber is the equivalent shape. Choose it when the program is already written in an effect; the discipline is stricter than Future (exactly-once completion, explicit cancellation) but you own the runtime and its scheduler.
variants.code_sketch:
val reply: IO[Reply] =
  IO.async[Reply] { cb =>                 // cb is the completion callback token
    service.register(req, cb)             // call cb(Right(reply)) or cb(Left(error)) exactly once
  }
pitfalls: The callback must be invoked exactly once: a timeout path that also completes it breaks the runtime's contract, so guard completion with an atomic/cas.
Without IO.cancelable or a finalizer, abandoning the fiber leaves the registration and its state alive in the service.
